---
name: scroll-3d-experience-builder
description: Build premium scroll-driven web experiences — scroll-animated landing pages (GSAP ScrollTrigger, Lenis, pinned sections, parallax, video scrubbing), real-time 3D scenes (Three.js / React Three Fiber), interactive 3D object disassembly / exploded-view animations tied to scroll, and generating or optimizing GLB/GLTF 3D assets (procedural generation, GLTFExporter, gltf-transform, Draco compression). Use this whenever the user asks for a landing page with scroll animations, an "Apple-style" product page, a hero section that animates on scroll, an exploded view or teardown of a 3D object, a Three.js scene driven by scroll, a GLB/GLTF model to be created, converted, or compressed, or any web page where 3D or motion is the centerpiece — even if they never say "scroll-driven" or "Three.js" explicitly.
---

# Scroll & 3D Experience Builder

Build the class of web experience popularized by Apple product pages and awwwards-winning sites: the page scrolls, and something cinematic happens — sections pin and transform, a product rotates or explodes into its components, a pre-rendered video scrubs frame-by-frame, text and imagery choreograph themselves to scroll position.

This skill covers three domains that usually appear together. Read only the reference file(s) the task needs:

| The user wants... | Read |
|---|---|
| A scroll-animated landing page (pinning, parallax, reveals, horizontal scroll, video scrubbing, smooth scroll) | `references/landing-pages.md` |
| A 3D model created, generated procedurally, converted, optimized, or compressed (GLB/GLTF) | `references/glb-assets.md` |
| An object that disassembles / explodes / reassembles as the user scrolls (real-time 3D or scrubbed video) | `references/disassembly.md` |

A full "product page with an exploding 3D model" job spans all three: source or generate the GLB first, build the disassembly scene second, wrap it in the landing-page scaffold last.

## Decision: real-time 3D vs. scrubbed video

This is the first fork in every 3D-on-scroll project, so decide it before writing code:

- **Real-time 3D (Three.js / React Three Fiber)** when the user needs interactivity (hover to highlight parts, click to select, free rotation), when no pre-rendered footage exists, or when the model is available/creatable as GLB. Works everywhere, no asset pipeline, fully dynamic — but visual fidelity is bounded by what runs at 60fps in a browser.
- **Scroll-scrubbed video** when photorealism matters more than interactivity and the user has (or can render) footage. A video is just a texture — it can show path-traced lighting no browser could compute live. The tradeoff: nothing is clickable, and the video must be encoded for scrubbing (see `references/landing-pages.md` § Video scrubbing — a normally-encoded MP4 stutters badly when scrubbed).
- **Hybrid**: scrubbed video for the cinematic hero, a lightweight real-time canvas lower on the page for the interactive configurator. Common on real product sites.

If the user hasn't specified and both are viable, ask — this choice changes the whole architecture.

## Core stack

Default to this stack unless the user's project dictates otherwise:

- **GSAP + ScrollTrigger** for scroll choreography. It is the industry standard because `scrub`, `pin`, and timeline sequencing solve 90% of scroll-animation problems declaratively. (GSAP is now 100% free including all plugins.)
- **Lenis** for smooth scrolling. Native scroll is quantized by wheel deltas; Lenis interpolates it, which makes scrubbed animation feel fluid. Always sync it to ScrollTrigger (snippet in `references/landing-pages.md`).
- **Three.js** for vanilla 3D; **React Three Fiber + drei** when the project is React. drei's `useGLTF`, `useScroll`, `Environment`, and `ScrollControls` remove most boilerplate.
- **gltf-transform CLI** for GLB optimization (Draco/meshopt compression, texture resizing, pruning).

In Claude.ai artifacts, import Three.js (r128) directly; note `OrbitControls` and `CapsuleGeometry` are unavailable there — use custom controls and Cylinder/Sphere geometry. For standalone HTML, load current Three.js via importmap from a CDN.

## Non-negotiables (apply to every build)

1. **Animate only `transform` and `opacity`** in DOM animations. Animating layout properties (top, width, margin) forces reflow every frame and kills the 60fps feel that defines this genre.
2. **Store original state before animating 3D nodes.** On GLB load, clone each mesh's `position`/`rotation` into `userData`. Every scroll handler must compute *from the original*, never accumulate onto the current value — accumulation drifts and the model never reassembles cleanly.
3. **Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.** Gate scroll animations behind a media-query check and provide a static fallback. This is an accessibility requirement, not a nicety.
4. **Kill and rebuild ScrollTriggers on unmount/resize** (`ScrollTrigger.refresh()`, and in React, `gsap.context()` with cleanup). Stale triggers are the #1 source of "the page jumps around" bugs.
5. **Budget the GLB.** For a hero model: ≤ 5 MB compressed, ≤ 150k triangles, ≤ 2048px textures. Anything heavier needs the optimization pass in `references/glb-assets.md`.
6. **Design mobile-first for scroll length.** A 400vh pinned section that feels cinematic on desktop feels endless on a phone; shorten scroll distances and simplify effects below ~768px.

## Workflow

1. **Clarify the centerpiece.** What object/story is the scroll telling? How many "scenes" (pinned sections)? Real-time or video (fork above)?
2. **Secure the asset.** Existing GLB from the user → validate and optimize. No asset → generate procedurally or source one (`references/glb-assets.md`). Video route → confirm footage exists or is renderable.
3. **Build the scroll skeleton first** — plain colored placeholder sections with working pin/scrub behavior. Getting the scroll math right before adding visuals saves rework.
4. **Add the 3D/video layer** into the skeleton.
5. **Polish**: easing, stagger, reduced-motion fallback, mobile pass, loading states (a 3D page must never show a blank canvas while the GLB streams — show a progress indicator).
6. **Deliver** as an artifact (single-file HTML or React) or project files, per context.

## Bundled scripts

- `scripts/generate_glb.py` — procedurally builds parameterized GLB models (phone, gearbox, drone, generic multi-part device) with named, separated parts ready for disassembly animation. Use it whenever no model asset exists; parts being *separate named meshes* is the property disassembly needs, and downloaded models often lack it. Run `python scripts/generate_glb.py --help` for options.
- `scripts/optimize_glb.sh` — one-shot gltf-transform pipeline (prune → weld → draco → texture resize). Requires Node; falls back with instructions if unavailable.

# Scroll-Driven Landing Pages Patterns and code for scroll-choreographed landing pages. Contents: 1. [Page architecture](#1-page-architecture) 2. [Setup: GSAP + ScrollTrigger + Lenis](#2-setup) 3. [Pattern: pinned scene with scrubbed timeline](#3-pinned-scene) 4. [Pattern: parallax layers](#4-parallax) 5. [Pattern: text & element reveals](#5-reveals) 6. [Pattern: horizontal scroll section](#6-horizontal-scroll) 7. [Pattern: scroll-scrubbed video](#7-video-scrubbing) 8. [Pattern: scroll progress + snapping](#8-progress-and-snap) 9. [CSS-only alternative (scroll-driven animations API)](#9-css-only) 10. [Performance & accessibility checklist](#10-checklist) --- ## 1. Page architecture Think of the page as a sequence of *scenes*, each one of: - **Flow scene** — normal content, scrolls by, gets entrance reveals. - **Pinned scene** — a `position: sticky`/pinned viewport-height stage; a tall spacer behind it converts scroll distance into animation progress. This is where the cinematic stuff happens. - **Transition scene** — short overlap where one scene hands off to the next (crossfade, scale, clip-path wipe). The universal skeleton for a pinned scene: ```html
``` `height: 300vh` means "this scene owns 2 extra viewport-heights of scroll" — that surplus is the scrub range. Rule of thumb: 100vh of extra height per ~2 seconds of perceived animation. More height = slower, more deliberate motion. ## 2. Setup ```html ``` ```javascript gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger); // Lenis smooth scroll, synced to ScrollTrigger — use exactly this wiring. const lenis = new Lenis({ lerp: 0.1 }); lenis.on('scroll', ScrollTrigger.update); gsap.ticker.add((time) => lenis.raf(time * 1000)); gsap.ticker.lagSmoothing(0); ``` Why the sync matters: Lenis animates `scrollTop` itself, so ScrollTrigger must be told about every interpolated frame (`lenis.on('scroll', ...)`) and driven by GSAP's ticker, or scrubbed animations judder against the smoothed scroll. React: wrap animation code in `useGSAP` (from `@gsap/react`) or `gsap.context()` inside `useEffect`, and return `ctx.revert()` for cleanup. Never create ScrollTriggers outside a cleanup scope in React — hot reload will stack duplicates. ## 3. Pinned scene The workhorse pattern — pin a stage and scrub a whole timeline across the scene's scroll distance: ```javascript const tl = gsap.timeline({ scrollTrigger: { trigger: '.scene', start: 'top top', end: 'bottom bottom', scrub: 0.5, // 0.5s catch-up; use `true` for 1:1 lock // pin: '.stage', // only if NOT using position: sticky in CSS } }); tl.fromTo('.product', { scale: 0.6, y: 100 }, { scale: 1, y: 0, duration: 2 }) .fromTo('.headline', { opacity: 0, y: 40 }, { opacity: 1, y: 0 }, '<0.5') .to('.product', { rotate: 8, x: '20vw', duration: 2 }) .fromTo('.feature-card', { opacity: 0, x: -60 }, { opacity: 1, x: 0, stagger: 0.2 }, '<'); ``` Notes: - Prefer CSS `position: sticky` over ScrollTrigger's `pin` when possible — sticky is compositor-handled and never causes the layout jump `pin-spacer` sometimes does. Use `pin` when you need pinning that CSS sticky can't express (pin across multiple parents). - Timeline `duration` values are *relative weights*, not seconds, when scrubbed — a duration-2 tween takes twice the scroll distance of a duration-1 tween. - `scrub: 0.5` (slight smoothing) almost always feels better than `scrub: true`. ## 4. Parallax Depth from differential speed. Give layers a `data-speed` and one loop handles all of them: ```javascript gsap.utils.toArray('[data-speed]').forEach((el) => { gsap.to(el, { y: () => (1 - parseFloat(el.dataset.speed)) * ScrollTrigger.maxScroll(window) * 0.1, ease: 'none', scrollTrigger: { trigger: el, start: 'top bottom', end: 'bottom top', scrub: true } }); }); ``` `data-speed="0.8"` drifts slower than scroll (background), `1.2` faster (foreground). Keep offsets subtle (≤ 15% of viewport) — heavy parallax reads as gimmicky and causes motion sickness. ## 5. Reveals Entrance animations for flow scenes. Batch them; do not create one ScrollTrigger per element by hand: ```javascript ScrollTrigger.batch('.reveal', { start: 'top 85%', once: true, onEnter: (batch) => gsap.fromTo(batch, { opacity: 0, y: 50 }, { opacity: 1, y: 0, duration: 0.8, stagger: 0.12, ease: 'power3.out' }) }); ``` For headline text, split into lines/words first (SplitText plugin, now free; or split manually) and stagger with a slight `yPercent: 100` + `clip-path` mask on the parent — the "text rising out of nothing" look. ## 6. Horizontal scroll Vertical scroll translating a horizontal track — the panel-gallery pattern: ```javascript const track = document.querySelector('.h-track'); // display:flex, width: max-content gsap.to(track, { x: () => -(track.scrollWidth - window.innerWidth), ease: 'none', scrollTrigger: { trigger: '.h-section', start: 'top top', end: () => '+=' + (track.scrollWidth - window.innerWidth), // scroll distance = overflow scrub: true, pin: true, invalidateOnRefresh: true, } }); ``` Making `end` equal the horizontal overflow gives a natural 1:1 feel. `invalidateOnRefresh` recomputes the function-based values on resize — required, or resizing breaks the section. ## 7. Video scrubbing Scroll position drives `video.currentTime`. The photorealistic route for product cinematics. ```html
``` ```javascript const video = document.getElementById('scrub'); video.addEventListener('loadedmetadata', () => { gsap.to(video, { currentTime: video.duration, ease: 'none', scrollTrigger: { trigger: '.video-scene', start: 'top top', end: 'bottom bottom', scrub: 0.5 } }); }); ``` **The encoding is the make-or-break detail.** Default MP4s have keyframes every ~250 frames; seeking must decode from the last keyframe, so scrubbing stutters. Re-encode with every frame a keyframe: ```bash ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vf scale=1920:-2 -an \ -c:v libx264 -g 1 -keyint_min 1 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 21 -movflags +faststart output.mp4 ``` `-g 1` = all-keyframe (large file but instant seeks; keep clips ≤ 10s / ≤ 1080p). `-an` strips audio (scrubbed video must be muted anyway). For very long sequences, the higher-fidelity alternative is an image-sequence canvas: preload JPEG frames, draw the frame indexed by scroll progress to a `` — smoother than any video seek, at the cost of bandwidth. iOS note: `playsinline` + `muted` are mandatory or the video won't render inline; also call `video.play().then(() => video.pause())` on first touch to unlock seeking on some Safari versions. ## 8. Progress and snap Progress bar: `scrollTrigger: { ..., onUpdate: self => bar.style.transform = `scaleX(${self.progress})` }`. Snapping between scenes: add `snap: 1 / (sceneCount - 1)` to a full-page ScrollTrigger, or per-scene `snap: { snapTo: [0, 1], duration: 0.4 }`. Use sparingly — snap fights smooth-scroll libraries; test with Lenis enabled. ## 9. CSS-only For simple reveals/parallax without JS, modern CSS scroll-driven animations work in Chromium/Firefox (check current Safari support before relying on it): ```css @keyframes fade-up { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(40px); } } .reveal { animation: fade-up linear both; animation-timeline: view(); animation-range: entry 0% entry 60%; } ``` Use as progressive enhancement; keep GSAP for anything sequenced or pinned. ## 10. Checklist - [ ] Only `transform`/`opacity` animated; `will-change: transform` on the few heavy movers (not globally). - [ ] `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` → disable scrub/pin, show content statically: ```javascript if (window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches) { // skip animation setup; ensure all .reveal elements are visible } ``` - [ ] All function-based ScrollTrigger values use `invalidateOnRefresh: true`. - [ ] `ScrollTrigger.refresh()` after fonts/images/GLBs load (late layout shifts break trigger positions). - [ ] Mobile pass: shorter scene heights (≤ 200vh), no horizontal-scroll pin under 768px (convert to swipe/stack), test on a real phone — DevTools emulation lies about scroll performance. - [ ] Content readable with JS disabled (animations enhance, never gate, the content).

# GLB / GLTF Asset Generation & Optimization

How to produce, convert, and optimize the 3D assets the other patterns consume. Contents:

1. [Which route to take](#1-which-route)
2. [Procedural generation in Python (trimesh)](#2-python-trimesh)
3. [Procedural generation in the browser (Three.js GLTFExporter)](#3-threejs-exporter)
4. [Blender headless scripting](#4-blender)
5. [Converting other formats to GLB](#5-conversion)
6. [Optimization pipeline (gltf-transform)](#6-optimization)
7. [Loading GLBs correctly (centering, original positions, draco)](#7-loading)
8. [Asset requirements for disassembly](#8-disassembly-requirements)

---

## 1. Which route

- **User has a model** (GLB, FBX, OBJ, STL...) → convert if needed (§5), validate part structure (§8), optimize (§6).
- **No model, geometric/mechanical object** (device, gearbox, drone, abstract product) → generate procedurally. `scripts/generate_glb.py` covers common archetypes; extend it or write trimesh code (§2) for custom shapes. Procedural wins for disassembly because you control part separation and naming exactly.
- **No model, organic/branded object** (a specific sneaker, a character) → procedural won't cut it; tell the user they need a real asset (their own render/scan, a purchased or CC-licensed model) and offer a stylized procedural stand-in meanwhile. Do not fabricate links to model marketplaces from memory — search if sourcing is needed.

## 2. Python (trimesh)

The fastest server-side route. `pip install trimesh numpy pillow --break-system-packages` (pygltflib not needed; trimesh exports GLB natively).

```python
import trimesh
import numpy as np

parts = {}

# Body: rounded box via a scaled sphere-ish primitive or plain box
body = trimesh.creation.box(extents=[2.0, 0.3, 4.0])
body.visual = trimesh.visual.TextureVisuals(
    material=trimesh.visual.material.PBRMaterial(
        baseColorFactor=[0.15, 0.15, 0.17, 1.0], metallicFactor=0.9, roughnessFactor=0.35))
parts['body'] = body

# Screen: thin box floated just above
screen = trimesh.creation.box(extents=[1.85, 0.02, 3.8])
screen.apply_translation([0, 0.17, 0])
screen.visual = trimesh.visual.TextureVisuals(
    material=trimesh.visual.material.PBRMaterial(
        baseColorFactor=[0.02, 0.02, 0.05, 1.0], metallicFactor=0.1, roughnessFactor=0.05))
parts['screen'] = screen

# Camera module: cylinder
cam = trimesh.creation.cylinder(radius=0.25, height=0.1, sections=48)
cam.apply_transform(trimesh.transformations.rotation_matrix(np.pi/2, [1,0,0]))
cam.apply_translation([-0.6, 0.2, -1.5])
parts['camera_module'] = cam

scene = trimesh.Scene()
for name, mesh in parts.items():
    scene.add_geometry(mesh, node_name=name, geom_name=name)  # names survive into the GLB
scene.export('device.glb')
```

The two things that matter for downstream animation: **each part is its own named node** (add via `node_name=`), and **the assembly is modeled in its assembled position** — the disassembly code derives explode vectors from those positions.

PBR materials: always set `metallicFactor`/`roughnessFactor`, not just color. An all-default-material model looks like grey clay under `Environment` lighting.

## 3. Three.js GLTFExporter

For generating assets client-side (e.g., inside an artifact that both builds and displays the model):

```javascript
import { GLTFExporter } from 'three/addons/exporters/GLTFExporter.js';

const group = new THREE.Group();
const body = new THREE.Mesh(
  new THREE.BoxGeometry(2, 0.3, 4),
  new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0x26262b, metalness: 0.9, roughness: 0.35 }));
body.name = 'body';
group.add(body);
// ...more named parts...

new GLTFExporter().parse(group,
  (glb) => {  // ArrayBuffer when binary: true
    const blob = new Blob([glb], { type: 'model/gltf-binary' });
    const a = Object.assign(document.createElement('a'),
      { href: URL.createObjectURL(blob), download: 'model.glb' });
    a.click();
  },
  (err) => console.error(err),
  { binary: true });
```

Often you can skip the export entirely: if the generated model is only used in the same page, keep it as a live `THREE.Group` and animate it directly — GLB is for persistence and hand-off.

## 4. Blender

When quality demands real modeling ops (bevels, booleans, subdivision), script Blender headless:

```bash
blender --background --python make_model.py
```

```python
# make_model.py
import bpy
bpy.ops.object.select_all(action='SELECT'); bpy.ops.object.delete()

bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cylinder_add(radius=1, depth=0.4)
gear = bpy.context.active_object
gear.name = 'gear_main'
bpy.ops.object.modifier_add(type='BEVEL')
gear.modifiers['Bevel'].width = 0.02

bpy.ops.export_scene.gltf(filepath='out.glb', export_format='GLB', export_yup=True)
```

Only reach for Blender if it's installed (`which blender`) — do not install it ad hoc in constrained environments; trimesh covers most procedural needs.

## 5. Conversion

- OBJ/STL/PLY/DAE → GLB: trimesh one-liner — `trimesh.load('in.obj').export('out.glb')` (loads as a Scene when the file has groups; part names carry over from OBJ `o`/`g` groups).
- FBX → GLB: `npx fbx2gltf in.fbx -o out.glb` or Blender import/export (FBX is proprietary; trimesh can't read it).
- USDZ → GLB: Blender 4.x imports USD.
- Always **GLB over GLTF+bin+textures** for the web: one file, one request, no broken relative paths.

## 6. Optimization

Run every production GLB through gltf-transform (`npm i -g @gltf-transform/cli`), or use `scripts/optimize_glb.sh` which wraps this:

```bash
gltf-transform prune in.glb tmp1.glb              # drop unused nodes/materials/accessors
gltf-transform weld tmp1.glb tmp2.glb             # merge duplicate vertices
gltf-transform resize tmp2.glb tmp3.glb --width 2048 --height 2048
gltf-transform draco tmp3.glb out.glb             # geometry compression, typically 5-10x
```

Guidance:
- **Draco** for hero models loaded once (best ratio, small decode cost). **Meshopt** (`gltf-transform meshopt`) when many models load or decode speed matters.
- Draco'd GLBs require wiring a decoder at load time (§7) — if you compress, you must also update the loader, or the model silently fails to load.
- Inspect before/after: `gltf-transform inspect out.glb` reports triangle counts, texture sizes, and total size. Target for a hero model: ≤ 5 MB, ≤ 150k tris.
- If a downloaded model is one merged mesh, no amount of optimization helps disassembly — see §8.

## 7. Loading

The canonical load sequence — centering, scaling, and snapshotting originals — used by everything downstream:

```javascript
import { GLTFLoader } from 'three/addons/loaders/GLTFLoader.js';
import { DRACOLoader } from 'three/addons/loaders/DRACOLoader.js';

const loader = new GLTFLoader();
const draco = new DRACOLoader();
draco.setDecoderPath('https://www.gstatic.com/draco/versioned/decoders/1.5.7/');
loader.setDRACOLoader(draco);   // harmless if the GLB isn't draco'd; required if it is

loader.load(url, (gltf) => {
  const model = gltf.scene;

  // 1. Center on origin and normalize scale to a known size
  const box = new THREE.Box3().setFromObject(model);
  const center = box.getCenter(new THREE.Vector3());
  const size = box.getSize(new THREE.Vector3()).length();
  model.position.sub(center);
  model.scale.setScalar(4 / size);   // model now fits a ~4-unit sphere

  // 2. Snapshot original transforms BEFORE any animation touches them
  model.traverse((child) => {
    if (child.isMesh) {
      child.userData.originalPosition = child.position.clone();
      child.userData.originalQuaternion = child.quaternion.clone();
    }
  });

  scene.add(model);
}, (xhr) => updateProgressBar(xhr.loaded / xhr.total),   // never leave a blank canvas
   (err) => showFallback(err));
```

React Three Fiber equivalent: `const { scene } = useGLTF(url)` (draco handled automatically), then do the same centering/snapshot inside a `useMemo` keyed on `scene`. Preload with `useGLTF.preload(url)`.

## 8. Disassembly requirements

Before promising a disassembly animation, verify the asset can support it:

1. **Separate meshes per part.** `model.traverse` and count meshes — 1 mesh = no disassembly without re-authoring. Fixes: regenerate procedurally, split in Blender (`P` → separate by loose parts), or fall back to the video method.
2. **Meaningful names** (`battery`, `top_case`) enable hover labels and per-part choreography. Rename in Blender or map by index if names are `mesh_0, mesh_1...`.
3. **Sane pivots.** Parts whose local origin is wildly offset from their geometry explode in weird directions; the loader pattern in §7 plus explode vectors computed from *world-space bounding-box centers* (see `references/disassembly.md`) sidesteps most pivot problems.
